segments.text: Big idea.
On the night Babylon fell, God weighed a king who had sinned against what he knew and ended
his kingdom.
John 5.22 says, the Father has given all judgment to the Son.
Jesus Christ is also the one who offers the only thing that can cover us when we are weighed,
his own perfect righteousness.
From the Last Sitting, Sitting 4.
In Chapter 4, Nebuchadnezzar learned that heaven rules.
After seven years of living like an animal because of his pride, he lifted his eyes and
blessed the Most High, Daniel 4.32-37.
He published that confession to every nation.
One generation later, Belshazzar sits in the same palace and acts as if the Most High does
not exist.
The Illusion of Invulnerability
Daniel 5.1-3
Babylon the Night of the Fall
In 539 BC, the combined Mado-Persian army under Cyrus the Great and his general, Ughbaru,
surrounded the city of Babylon.
Outside the towering fortifications, an empire was crumbling.
Inside, King Belshazzar, who ruled in Babylon alongside his father, Nebaius, main point
one explains, hosted a lavish, drunken banquet for a thousand of his highest nobles, along
with his wives and concubines.
Daniel 5.1-3
Babylon was considered impregnable.
Its monumental double walls were wide enough for multiple chariots to pass, and the Euphrates
River ran directly beneath the water gates, providing an endless water supply and deep
moats.
Belshazzar saw no problem in having a party while the enemy surrounds the city.
In an act of drunken insolence, he defied both the encircling armies outside and the
God of heaven above.
Main point one.
Belshazzar and the historical accuracy of Scripture
For a century, 19th-century critics claimed that the Book of Daniel was historical fiction
and that Belshazzar never existed.
Their reason was that the Greek historians in the Babylonian king lists named Nebaiusus
as the last king of Babylon and never mentioned to Belshazzar.
Archaeology has completely dismantled that skepticism.
The Nabonidus Cylinders of Ur.
In 1854, J.G. Taylor dug up small clay cylinders written in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped
writing of ancient Babylon.
They hold a prayer by Nabonidus for his eldest son, Belsar Usur, which is the
Babylonian form of the name Belshazzar.
So the king's son was real.
What an ancient Babylonian poem says about Nabonidus, Nabonidus made his home in
Taima, also spelled Taima, a desert town in Arabia for 10 years.
He left the kingship and the defense of Babylon to his eldest son, Belshazzar.
The third ruler, Precision.
Two men held power at the same time, a father and his son.
This is called a co-regency.
It explains why Belshazzar offered to make Daniel the third ruler in the kingdom,
Daniel 5, 16, 29.
Nabonidus was first, Belshazzar was second, and the highest office left for
Daniel was third.
History, Daniel 5 calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's father, Daniel 5, 2, 11, 18, 22.
In the Bible, father and son can mean an earlier and a later king of the same line.
So grandson in this sitting means a later king of Nebuchadnezzar's dynasty,
not necessarily a child's birth record.
The chapter hangs on a king who knew the family lesson and
still used God's cups to praise idols.
Main point two, the anatomy of sacrilege and sinning against light,
Daniel 5, 6, 23.
As the wine flowed, Belshazzar ordered the sacred gold and
silver vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar from Yahweh's temple in Jerusalem
to be brought into the banquet hall.
The king, his princes, his wives, and his concubines drank from those consecrated
cups while singing praises to the gods of gold and of silver,
of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.
This was not merely bad manners, it was deliberate sacrilege.
He took what had been set apart for God and used it in a proud feast.
Revelation later pictures Babylon as a woman arrayed in gold and precious stones,
drunk with the blood of saints, Revelation 17, 4-6.
The parallel is that pattern, wealth used against what is holy and
against the saints, desecrating the consecrated.
Sacrilege is taking that which has been set apart exclusively for
the holy worship of God and dragging it into common,
self-serving, or demonic usage, defying the living God.
By praising idols using the very vessels designed for Yahweh sanctuary,
Belshazzar staged an intentional theological provocation,
declaring Babylon's idols superior to the God of Israel.
Sinning against known revelation.
When Daniel was summoned to read the writing on the wall,
the next point explains it, he first gave the king a harsh charge,
Daniel 5, 18-23.
Daniel reminded Belshazzar of how God had humbled his grandfather,
Nebuchadnezzar, into the dust until he repented.
Daniel looked the young monarch in the eyes and said,
and thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart,
though thou newest all this, Daniel 5, 22.
Belshazzar's sin was worse because he knew better.
Light here means knowledge of God.
He had seen what happened to a proud king before him and
chose not to learn from it.
Luke 12, 48 states the principle,
unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
That is why judgment fell so swiftly.
We have come to the first checkpoint.
Main point three, the handwriting on the plaster,
the divine audit.
The revelry halted abruptly when a mysterious hand appeared,
writing on the plaster of the wall
over against the candlestick, Daniel 5, 5.
Belshazzar was terrified.
The king's countenance was changed
and his thoughts troubled him,
so that the joints of his loins were loosed
and his knees smote one against another, Daniel 5, 6.
The writing was four words,
Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin, Daniel 5, 25.
Mene is written twice and Upharsin means and Parson,
a form of Paris.
These are Aramaic words,
the everyday language of the empire.
Daniel reads them as numbered, weighed, and divided,
Daniel 5, 26 through 28.
Mene, numbered, the word sounds like the Aramaic word
for counting.
God has numbered the kingdom and finished it, Daniel 5, 26.
This throne's account is closed in a night.
Tekel, weighed, the word sounds like the Aramaic word
for weighing, the shekel is a weight.
You have been placed upon the moral balances
of divine justice and have been found wanting.
Paris, divided, a word play in Aramaic.
Paris means divided and it sounds like Paris,
the word for the Persians.
The Babylonian empire was to be dismantled
and handed to the Medo-Persians.
Text, every throne, institution, and individual life
stands before an open ledger in heaven.
God numbers the days of power, weighs moral character,
and as at Belshazzar's feast,
can finish a kingdom in a night.
Daniel 5, 26 through 30.
We have come to the second checkpoint.
Main point four, the fall of Babylon
and the precision of prophecy.
Daniel 5, 30, in that night.
16 Tishri, 12 October 539 BC.
That very night, Daniel 5, 30,
Babylon fell without a battle.
Ughbaru's troops entered on the 16th day
of the month Tishri, 12 October 539 BC.
Persian engineers diverted the waters of the Euphrates River
into an artificial basin.
Persian soldiers marched down the depleted riverbed,
passed through the bronze river gates,
left unlocked during the drunken festivities
and seized the palace.
That very night, Belshazzar was slain
and Darius the Mede took the kingdom.
Daniel 5, 30 to 31.
The Bible does not say how Darius relates to Cyrus
and the next sitting looks at that question.
A Babylonian chronicle confirms the sudden fall.
Ughbaru and the troops of Cyrus entered Babylon
without battle.
The gold kingdom gave way to the silver kingdom
in a single evening.
In the dream of Daniel 2,
Babylon was the head of gold, Daniel 2 38.
And a second kingdom, the chest and arms of silver,
Daniel 2 32, was to come after it, Daniel 39.
This reading takes that second kingdom to be Medo-Persia.
So this night is that change.
Main point five, the redemptive core.
Cyrus as type and Christ as the true deliverer.
The fall of Babylon is not merely an ancient political event.
It is also a type, an earlier picture of a later act of God.
Cyrus was named God's anointed,
took Babylon and freed the captives.
Christ is the greater anointed one
who frees his people from sin.
Revelation uses the name Babylon
for the final power that stands against God.
In Revelation 18, shows that Babylon falling
as old Babylon fell.
One, Cyrus the anointed deliverer.
God called Cyrus his shepherd, Isaiah 44 28.
And his anointed, Hebrew Mashiach, Isaiah 45 1.
The only pagan ruler in scripture to receive this title.
Cyrus prefigured the Messiah
by breaking the power of the oppressor,
setting God's captive people free
and ordering the restoration of the temple.
Isaiah 44 28, Isaiah 45 13.
Isaiah wrote this in the days of King Hezekiah
more than a century before Cyrus took Babylon.
Two, Christ the ultimate auditor and king.
In John 5 22, Jesus declared,
for the father judgeth no man
but hath committed all judgment unto the son.
The same Christ to whom the father has committed
all judgment will weigh every life.
Revelation 20 11 to 12.
Belshazzar's night shows that heaven already audits thrones.
Three, found wanting yet covered
by the righteousness Christ gives.
Belshazzar was weighed and found wanting.
Thou art weighed in the balances and art found wanting.
The same verdict stands over everyone God weighs
by his holy law because all have sinned
and come short of the glory of God.
Romans 3 23.
Sin here means falling short of what God asks.
Here's the glory of the gospel.
On the cross of Calvary,
Jesus Christ bore the full weight
of divine justice for our sins.
When a sinner repents and places their faith in Christ,
his perfect righteousness is credited to our account.
To Corinthians 5 21, Romans 5 18 to 19.
Righteousness means being right with God
and credited means counted as ours.
Faith is how we accept this gift.
Romans 4 5 says that to the one who believeth on him
that justifieth the ungodly,
his faith is counted for righteousness.
When God weighs the believer,
we are no longer found wanting.
We possess the infinite unassailable moral weight
of the son of God himself, Christ.
If you stand in your own merit, you are found wanting.
If you are clothed in the righteousness of Christ,
you can stand before the throne with exceeding joy.
In plain words, God had already numbered,
weighed and divided Babylon
and the writing on the wall only announced the verdict.
Interpretation.
The writing on the plaster was not a prediction.
It was a receipt.
Babylon's end had already been decided.
In the four Aramaic words announced a verdict
that was complete before the hand appeared.
Daniel 5 25 to 28.
Read the three words as a plain sequence, numbered.
God has counted the days this throne would last
and the count is finished.
Wade, the king himself was set on the scales
against God's standard and the standard did not move.
Divided, the kingdom was broken up
and handed to another power that same night,
which the words show by the sound of Perez,
close to Peros, the word for the Persians.
Why did this happen to this king and not to another?
Daniel tells him the reason to his face.
Belshazzar knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar
and he did not humble his heart, Daniel 5 22.
He took the cups that belonged to God's house
and used them to praise gods of silver and gold,
Daniel 5 23.
So this was not an ordinary defeat in war.
It was judgment on a man who had been handed the truth
and treated it as a decoration.
The bottom line is uncomfortable and simple.
Numbered, weighed and divided is how the chapter
describes God's government of a life
as well as of an empire.
To be numbered is to admit your days
are not your own to spend.
To be weighed is to admit your own merit
will not balance the account.
That is why this book turns in every sitting
to one whose righteousness is given rather than earned.
We have come to the third checkpoint.
Practical application,
navigating the feasts of modern Babylon.
Belshazzar's downfall provides sobering warnings
for the modern world.
Beware of feasting on borrowed holy things.
The world takes what belongs to God
such as truth, time and worship
and treats it as a plaything for selfish pleasure.
God will not be mocked.
Whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap.
Galatians 6, 7.
Do not presume upon past mercy.
Belshazzar knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar
and presumed he could escape judgment.
He did not humble his heart.
Daniel 5, 22.
In that refusal was the charge against him.
Truth that we know and ignore
counts against us in the same way.
Anchor your life in Christ's righteousness.
Worldly security can vanish overnight
just as Babylon fell in a single hour.
Revelation 18, 10.
The only refuge from the divine scale
is the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
The principle to remember,
God weighs every throne and every life
and only the righteousness of Christ
can cover what is found wanting.
Test any reading with four questions.
Text, does Daniel 5, 22 say Belshazzar knew all this
and still did not humble his heart?
History, do the ancient Babylonian records
confirm the co-regency and a fall without battle?
Interpretation, Armenae, Tikal, and Peres,
the verbs numbered, weighed, and divided.
Christ, does the scale find you wanting in yourself
or covered by the righteousness of the sun?
Christ overthrows spiritual Babylon, Revelation 18,
conquers sin, conquers death, 1 Corinthians 15, 26,
and the new Jerusalem comes down from God, Revelation 21, 2.
On our own merit, the verdict is tekel, found wanting.
On the cross, Christ bore the full weight of justice.
His righteousness is credited to the believer,
2 Corinthians 5, 21.
When God weighs those who trust the sun,
they possess the moral weight of Christ himself.
